scenes.text: Water on a scorching pan should vanish in a flash. Instead, it skates around like it's alive.
label: LEIDENFROST EFFECT
Water on a very hot pan

hud.label: Pan temperature
hud.sub: at or above the Leidenfrost point

scenes.text: Normally, a drop touching hot metal boils away fast. Here, it survives.
Keep heating, and something flips. Past a certain heat, a hotter pan makes the drop last longer.
Zoom in on that gap. The drop sits on a vapour cushion about a tenth of a millimetre thick, and the steam keeps escaping sideways while the bottom of the drop keeps boiling to refill it.
scenes.code:
title=Text("INSIDE THE GAP",font_size=40,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
plate=Rectangle(width=10,height=0.8,color=RED,fill_color=RED_E,fill_opacity=1).shift(DOWN*2.2)
pl=Text("HOT PLATE",font_size=30,color=WHITE).move_to(plate)
drop=Circle(radius=1.3,color=BLUE,fill_color=BLUE_E,fill_opacity=0.8).shift(UP*0.2)
gap=Rectangle(width=3.2,height=0.18,color=YELLOW,fill_color=YELLOW,fill_opacity=0.5).shift(DOWN*1.6)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(plate),FadeIn(pl),FadeIn(drop),run_time=1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(gap),run_time=1)
al=[Arrow(LEFT*0.2+DOWN*1.6,LEFT*3.2+DOWN*1.6,color=YELLOW,buff=0),Arrow(RIGHT*0.2+DOWN*1.6,RIGHT*3.2+DOWN*1.6,color=YELLOW,buff=0)]
self.play(*[GrowArrow(a) for a in al],run_time=1.5)
lab=Text("VAPOUR CUSHION ~0.1 mm",font_size=34,color=YELLOW).move_to(DOWN*3.1)
wl=Text("WATER DROP",font_size=30,color=WHITE).move_to(drop)
self.play(FadeIn(lab),FadeIn(wl),run_time=1)
self.play(*[a.animate.shift(RIGHT*0.3 if i else LEFT*0.3) for i,a in enumerate(al)],run_time=1.5,rate_func=there_and_back)

scenes.question: What is holding this drop up?
scenes.heading: A DROP ON A HOT PLATE
scenes.text: Look at the gap. The bottom of the drop flash-boils and creates a thin layer of vapour, a fraction of a millimetre thick. The drop floats on its own steam. And steam conducts heat badly, so the drop barely heats up and lasts far longer.
Below roughly two hundred degrees, the drop touches and boils fast. Above it, the cushion forms, and the lifetime shoots up.
scenes.code:
title=Text("DROP LIFETIME vs PAN HEAT",font_size=40,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
ax=Axes(x_range=[100,400,100],y_range=[0,100,25],x_length=9,y_length=4,axis_config={"color":GREY_B,"include_numbers":True}).shift(DOWN*0.4)
xl=Text("pan temperature (deg C)",font_size=30).next_to(ax,DOWN)
yl=Text("lifetime",font_size=30).next_to(ax,LEFT).rotate(PI/2).shift(RIGHT*0.4)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(ax),FadeIn(xl),FadeIn(yl),run_time=1.5)
f=lambda x:(5+85*(x-100)/100*0 + 95*np.exp(-((x-100)/45)) *1.0) if x<200 else (10+ 80*((x-200)/200)**1.3)
c1=ax.plot(f,x_range=[100,199],color=BLUE,stroke_width=7,use_smoothing=False)
c2=ax.plot(f,x_range=[200,400],color=RED,stroke_width=7,use_smoothing=False)
self.play(Create(c1),run_time=2.5)
dot=Dot(ax.c2p(200,f(200)),color=YELLOW,radius=0.14)
lp=Text("LEIDENFROST POINT ~200 C",font_size=32,color=YELLOW).move_to(UP*1.6+LEFT*1.2)
self.play(FadeIn(dot),FadeIn(lp),run_time=1)
self.play(Create(c2),run_time=2.5)

scenes.text: Cooks use this without knowing the name. Flick water into a pan: if it sizzles away, the pan is warm. If it beads up and glides in one shiny ball, the pan is hot, past the Leidenfrost point.
label: THE COOK'S TEST
Dancing beads mean a very hot pan

scenes.label: JOHANN GOTTLOB LEIDENFROST, 1756
scenes.text: The effect carries the name of Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756.
Then, in 2015, UK physicists swapped water for a block of dry ice, frozen carbon dioxide.
Now drop a very hot metal ball in water. It wraps itself in vapour, until the film collapses.
label: HOT METAL IN WATER
Vapour film, then collapse

scenes.text: Dry ice never melts on hot metal. It sublimes, and rides on its own gas.
label: NATURE COMMUNICATIONS, 2015
Wells et al., lab footage

scenes.text: Cut ratchet teeth into the metal, and the escaping gas pushes the ice. It drives a rotor.
label: A HEAT ENGINE RUNNING ON ICE
Sublimation heat engine
scenes.fact: THE GAS CUSHION CAN PUSH,\NNOT JUST LIFT

scenes.text: Liquid nitrogen, at minus 196 degrees, skates the same way on a room-temperature floor. So when water dances on your pan, it is riding on its own steam. Subscribe for the next one.
label: LIQUID NITROGEN
Boils at about -196 °C

shorts.title: Dry Ice That Rides on Its Own Gas

scenes.text: This dry ice is minus seventy-eight degrees, and it is vanishing into thin air.
It never melts. It turns straight from solid to gas, a change called sublimation, here in a flood of fog.
Liquid nitrogen, far colder, boils off a desk the same way. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

youtube.title: The Hotter the Pan, the Longer Water Survives
youtube.description:
Hotter pan, longer life: water can float on its own steam, and a block of dry ice can spin a turbine. Here is the Leidenfrost effect, and the lab experiment that turned it into an engine.

In this video:
- Why a drop of water lasts longer on a hotter pan
- The vapour cushion under the drop
- The 2015 dry ice "sublimation heat engine"
- A hot ball in water, and liquid nitrogen on a desk

strategy.viewer: Curious adults who have seen water dance on a hot pan and wonder why it does not simply boil away.
strategy.hook: Water on a scorching pan should vanish in a flash, yet it skates around like it is alive.
strategy.promise: Why a hotter pan makes a drop live longer, and the lab experiment where dry ice drove an engine.
strategy.payoff: A drop on a very hot surface rides on a cushion of its own vapour (Leidenfrost effect); the same trick lets dry ice and liquid nitrogen glide, and the gas can even push a rotor.
strategy.takeaway: A drop on a hot pan floats on its own steam.
